summary.text: Xylem is one of the two types of transport tissue in vascular plants, the other being phloem.
Its basic function is to carry water upward from the roots to parts of the plant such as stems and leaves, and it also transports nutrients.
The best-known xylem tissue is wood, though xylem is found throughout a plant.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: From Ancient Greek xúlon, meaning wood

facts.label: Water carriers
facts.value: Tracheids and vessel elements, which differ in shape

facts.label: Softwood
facts.value: The secondary xylem of tall conifers

facts.label: Lifting height
facts.value: Transpirational pull can lift water as high as a hundred meters

items.prompt: Water evaporates from the leaves of a tall tree. What does that do to the water in the xylem?

options.label: It creates tension that pulls water up from the roots
It pushes water down toward the roots
It turns the water into sugar
It stops all flow until evening

items.explain: Evaporation from leaf cells creates a negative pressure that pulls water up from the roots and soil, and more is drawn up to replace what evaporates.

items.prompt: Early in the morning, before the stomata open, which force that moves sap is at its highest?

options.label: Transpirational pull from the leaves
Root pressure, which pushes sap up the xylem
The sugar pressure in the phloem
The weight of the water in the trunk

items.explain: Root pressure forces sap up the xylem and is highest in the morning before the stomata open and transpiration begins.

items.prompt: Why do plants that rely on transpirational pull need very narrow water-carrying tubes?

options.label: Wider tubes would let in too much light
Wider tubes would stop the roots taking up water
Wider tubes would risk cavitation breaking the water column
Wider tubes would fill with sugar from the phloem

items.explain: Transpirational pull requires that the vessels be very small in diameter, otherwise cavitation would break the water column.

items.prompt: A lumber yard sells softwood and hardwood. What plant tissue are both made of?

options.label: Secondary xylem
Phloem
Primary xylem only
Root hairs

items.explain: The secondary xylem of tall conifers is marketed as softwood, and that of many non-monocot angiosperm trees is marketed as hardwood.

items.prompt: Sugars made in the leaves are kept in the phloem. What does the xylem carry instead?

options.label: Mostly sugars, under pressures of several MPa
Mostly water and minerals, with a far lower load of solutes
Mostly gases taken in through the leaves
Mostly hormones sent down from the shoot

items.explain: The phloem holds the sugars, while the xylem carries a far lower load of solutes, namely water and minerals.

items.prompt: After an embolism has occurred in a plant's water-carrying tubes, what can the plant do?

options.label: Nothing, since the tubes are lost for good
Reverse the flow so water moves downward
Replace the tubes only by growing a new trunk
Refill the xylem and restore its function

items.explain: Even after an embolism has occurred, plants are able to refill the xylem and restore its functionality.

paragraphs.heading: What xylem is
paragraphs.text: Xylem is one of the two kinds of transport tissue in vascular plants; phloem is the other, and both belong to the vascular bundle. Its basic job is to carry water up from the roots to parts such as stems and leaves, and it moves nutrients too. The name comes from xúlon, the Ancient Greek word for wood. Wood is the best-known xylem, but xylem runs all through a plant. The Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli coined the words xylem and phloem in 1858.

paragraphs.heading: The cells inside
paragraphs.text: The most distinctive xylem cells are tracheary elements, long cells that carry water. Tracheids and vessel elements are told apart by shape. Vessel elements are the shorter ones, and they link end to end into long tubes called vessels. Wood also holds two other kinds of cells, parenchyma and fibers.

paragraphs.heading: Primary and secondary xylem
paragraphs.text: Primary xylem forms during primary growth from a tissue called procambium. It has two parts: protoxylem, and metaxylem, which develops later and has wider vessels and tracheids. Secondary xylem comes after the metaxylem. All of the roughly 600 conifer species have it, and the secondary xylem of tall conifers is sold as softwood. It is rare among monocots, but many other angiosperms grow into trees whose secondary xylem is sold as hardwood.

paragraphs.heading: Pulling water to the top
paragraphs.text: Water evaporates from the surfaces of cells inside the leaves, and this draws the water surface back into tiny pores in the cell walls. There it forms curved, dish-shaped surfaces called menisci. Water's strong surface tension tugs on these curves, which puts the water in the xylem under tension and pulls more up from the roots and soil. This transpirational pull can raise water as high as a hundred meters, to the top branches of a tree. It works only because the vessels are very narrow; wider ones would let cavitation break the column of water.

paragraphs.heading: A push from below
paragraphs.text: Roots can also push. When root cells have a more negative water potential than the soil, usually because they hold many dissolved substances, water enters them by osmosis. That builds a positive pressure that forces sap up the xylem toward the leaves, and it is strongest in the morning before the stomata open. Species differ: up to 145 kPa in Vitis riparia but about zero in Celastrus orbiculatus. Sometimes sap is even pushed out of a leaf through a hydathode, which is called guttation.

paragraphs.heading: Why the water column holds
paragraphs.text: The cohesion-tension theory explains how water climbs through the xylem against gravity, by the attraction between water molecules. John Joly and Henry Horatio Dixon put it forward in 1894. It has faced many objections, yet it is still the most widely accepted account of water transport in plants. The attraction comes from hydrogen bonds: the slightly negative oxygen atom of one water molecule bonds to a slightly positive hydrogen atom of the next.
